title: Bash Traps & Signals: Cleanup That Actually Runs
summary: A dense field guide to trapping signals in Bash — EXIT and ERR traps, temp-file cleanup, killing child processes, and handling Ctrl-C — from signal fundamentals through subshell pitfalls and production-grade patterns.

chapters.title: Signals 101: What Bash Is Reacting To
points: A signal is an async notification the kernel delivers to a process; the process runs a handler, ignores it, or dies with the default action
`kill -l` lists all signal names and numbers on the current system
SIGINT (2) = Ctrl-C from the terminal, sent to the whole foreground process group, not just your script
SIGTERM (15) = polite 'please exit', default of plain `kill PID`; SIGKILL (9) = unblockable, uncatchable, no cleanup runs
SIGHUP (1) = controlling terminal went away (SSH drop, terminal closed); SIGQUIT (3) = Ctrl-\, dumps core by default
Exit status encodes signal death as 128 + signal number: Ctrl-C gives 130, SIGTERM gives 143, SIGKILL gives 137
Only SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored — every cleanup design must assume they can happen
Bash also has pseudo-signals that aren't real signals: EXIT, ERR, DEBUG, RETURN — trap uses the same syntax for both
Signals arriving while a foreground command runs are handled AFTER that command completes, unless the command itself dies from it
`trap` with no arguments prints the currently installed traps in re-usable form: `trap -- 'cleanup' EXIT`
Process groups matter: Ctrl-C hits every process in the foreground group, so children may already be dying when your handler runs
Distinguish 'the terminal sent it' (SIGINT via Ctrl-C) from 'someone scripted it' (`kill -INT $$`) — same signal, same handler

chapters.title: trap: Syntax, Scope, and Reset
points: Form: `trap 'commands' SIGSPEC...` — the action string is re-evaluated each time the signal fires, not at trap-definition time
Single quotes vs double quotes: `trap "rm $tmp" EXIT` expands `$tmp` NOW; `trap 'rm $tmp' EXIT` expands at fire time — usually you want single quotes
`trap - SIGSPEC` restores the default action; `trap '' SIGSPEC` ignores the signal entirely and children inherit that ignore
Signal names work with or without the SIG prefix, and numbers work too: `trap cleanup INT`, `TERM`, `2`, `15` all valid
One trap per signal — a second `trap ... INT` silently replaces the first; there is no handler chaining
Best practice: point traps at a named function (`trap cleanup EXIT`) so logic is testable and not stuffed in a quoted string
`trap -p EXIT` prints just that trap; useful to save and restore a handler around a critical section
Traps are NOT inherited by subshells for ERR/DEBUG/RETURN unless `set -E`/`set -T` is on; EXIT traps also reset in subshells
Functions do not get their own trap scope by default — traps are per-shell, so a function's `trap` overwrites the script's
Command substitution `$(...)` runs a subshell with traps reset to default — a trap set there dies with the subshell
`trap` inside a `( ... )` subshell fires when the subshell exits, which is a useful scoped-cleanup trick
Multiple signals in one call: `trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM HUP` — the common four-signal safety net

chapters.title: The EXIT Trap: Cleanup That Always Runs
points: EXIT fires on ANY shell termination: normal end of script, explicit `exit`, `set -e` abort, or an uncaught fatal signal
Because EXIT covers signal-caused exits too, `trap cleanup EXIT` alone catches most cases — INT/TERM traps mainly add custom messaging
EXIT does NOT fire on SIGKILL (-9) or on a hard `exec` replacing the shell — design for the leak, don't assume you'll always clean
Set the trap IMMEDIATELY after creating the resource, never before it exists and never several lines later
Inside an EXIT trap, `$?` holds the script's exit status — capture it first: `local rc=$?` before running anything else
The exit status of the script is the status at trap entry, unless the trap itself calls `exit N` with a new value
EXIT handler code must be idempotent and non-failing: use `rm -f`, guard with `[[ -n $tmp ]]`, redirect noise to /dev/null
`set -e` does not apply to a failure inside the EXIT trap the way you expect — an error mid-cleanup can skip the rest; use `|| true`
Ordering: only one EXIT trap exists, so a multi-resource script needs one cleanup function that tears down in reverse creation order
A common pattern is a cleanup stack: append commands to an array, then have the EXIT trap iterate the array backwards
EXIT traps run in subshells too, so `( trap 'echo sub' EXIT; ... )` prints when the parentheses close
Careless `exit` inside a trap that also has traps set can recurse — reset the trap at the top of cleanup: `trap - EXIT`
code: `cleanup(){ local rc=$?; rm -rf "${tmpdir:-}"; exit "$rc"; }; trap cleanup EXIT`

chapters.title: Temp Files: Create, Trap, Delete
points: Never hardcode `/tmp/myfile.$$` — predictable names are a symlink-attack vector and collide across users
`mktemp` creates a file with a random name and 0600 permissions atomically; `mktemp -d` creates a 0700 directory
Prefer one temp DIRECTORY over many temp files: a single `rm -rf "$tmpdir"` cleans everything, one trap covers all
Idiom: `tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)` then immediately `trap 'rm -rf "$tmpdir"' EXIT`
Use a template for debuggability: `mktemp -d -t myscript.XXXXXX` so leaked dirs are traceable to the script
Quote the variable in the trap — an unquoted empty `$tmpdir` turns `rm -rf $tmpdir/` into `rm -rf /`, a classic catastrophic bug
Guard the removal: `[[ -n ${tmpdir:-} && -d $tmpdir ]] && rm -rf -- "$tmpdir"`
`TMPDIR` env var controls where mktemp puts things; honor it rather than assuming /tmp exists and is writable
Deleting an open file on Linux is safe — the inode survives until the fd closes, so cleanup can run while a reader still holds it
Alternative: `exec 3<>"$file"; rm "$file"` — the file is unlinked immediately and vanishes even on SIGKILL
Never `rm -rf` a path built from unvalidated user input inside a trap; the trap runs at the worst possible moment
On failure you often want the temp dir KEPT for debugging: `[[ $rc -eq 0 ]] && rm -rf "$tmpdir" || echo "kept: $tmpdir"`
Named pipes and lock files need the same treatment: `mkfifo` + trap, or `flock` on a file descriptor that closes on exit

chapters.title: Killing Children: Jobs, PIDs, and Process Groups
points: Background a job with `&`; `$!` holds its PID — capture it right away, it's overwritten by the next background job
Killing the parent does NOT kill children; orphaned children get reparented to init and keep running
`jobs -p` lists PIDs of this shell's jobs; `kill $(jobs -p)` is a quick but non-recursive sweep
Grandchildren are the real problem: killing a child that spawned its own children leaves the grandchildren alive
Process-group kill: `kill -- -$PGID` sends to the entire group; `kill -- -$$` targets the script's own group
Make your script its own group leader with `set -m` (job control) so group signaling doesn't hit the caller's shell
`pkill -P $$` kills direct children by parent PID; still not recursive without walking the tree
Two-phase kill is the correct pattern: send TERM, wait a grace period, then send KILL to whatever survives
`wait` blocks until children finish; `wait -n` returns when any one finishes; `wait $pid` gives that child's exit status
Important: `wait` is interruptible — a trapped signal arriving during `wait` runs the handler, then `wait` returns non-zero
`timeout 10 cmd` sends TERM at the deadline; `timeout -k 5 10 cmd` follows with KILL 5s later — reuse instead of hand-rolling
Disown (`disown -h %1`) removes a job from HUP delivery when you deliberately want it to survive the shell
code: `kill -TERM "$pid" 2>/dev/null; sleep 2; kill -KILL "$pid" 2>/dev/null; wait "$pid" 2>/dev/null`

chapters.title: Ctrl-C and Interrupt Handling
points: Ctrl-C sends SIGINT to the entire foreground process group — your script AND every child it started in the foreground
A script that traps INT but does not exit becomes un-interruptible from the keyboard — a serious usability bug
Correct interrupt semantics: clean up, then kill yourself with the same signal so the parent sees a real signal death
Self-signal idiom: `trap - INT; kill -INT "$$"` — restore the default, re-raise, so exit status is truly 130
Returning a plain `exit 1` from an INT trap lies to the caller: shell wrappers and CI can't tell interrupt from failure
`trap '' INT` makes a critical section uninterruptible; restore with `trap - INT` immediately after, and keep it short
Long-running loops should check a flag set by the handler rather than doing heavy work inside the handler itself
During a foreground child, SIGINT usually kills the child first; your trap runs after the child returns, so check `$?` for 130
`read -t` and `sleep` in the foreground are interruptible; use `sleep 30 & wait $!` so a trap can fire promptly during long waits
Double Ctrl-C should force-exit: count invocations, and on the second one skip graceful cleanup and hard-kill
SIGHUP handling matters for SSH sessions — trap HUP alongside INT/TERM, or use `nohup`/`setsid` to survive it deliberately
Ctrl-Z (SIGTSTP) is separate: it stops the process, and cleanup should NOT run — do not trap TSTP for cleanup

chapters.title: The ERR Trap and set -e
points: `trap handler ERR` fires when a command returns non-zero, following the same rules that would trigger `set -e`
ERR is a bash pseudo-signal, not POSIX — dash/sh will not honor it, so shebang must be `#!/usr/bin/env bash`
ERR does NOT fire for: conditions in `if`/`while`, operands of `&&`/`||`, any command negated with `!`, or when `set -e` rules exempt it
By default ERR traps are NOT inherited by functions, command substitutions, or subshells — `set -E` (`errtrace`) fixes that
`set -e` alone is unreliable: it silently skips failures inside conditions, and functions called in a test context lose it entirely
The strict-mode triple: `set -euo pipefail` — exit on error, error on unset variable, and propagate pipeline failures
Without `pipefail`, `false | true` succeeds — the pipeline's status is the last command's, so errors vanish mid-pipe
`PIPESTATUS` array holds each pipeline element's status; read it immediately, it's clobbered by the next command
Rich ERR handler: report `$?`, `$LINENO`, and `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}` plus `${FUNCNAME[@]}` for a usable stack trace
ERR and EXIT both fire on a `set -e` abort: ERR runs first for diagnostics, then EXIT runs for cleanup — split those jobs
Use `|| true` to deliberately exempt a command from `set -e` and ERR, and comment WHY, or you'll re-break it later
Explicit error checking (`cmd || die "msg"`) is more predictable than `set -e` for scripts where every failure has a distinct response
code: `set -Eeuo pipefail; trap 'echo "FAIL line $LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND (rc=$?)" >&2' ERR`

chapters.title: Subshells, Inheritance, and Where Traps Vanish
points: A subshell is a forked copy of the shell: `( ... )`, `$( ... )`, pipeline segments, and background `&` all create one
Rule: on fork, traps for signals that were CAUGHT are reset to default in the child; signals set to IGNORE stay ignored
This is why a trap set in `$(...)` never affects the parent, and why the parent's EXIT trap doesn't run when a subshell exits
`set -E` (errtrace) makes ERR traps inherit into functions, command substitutions, and subshells
`set -T` (functrace) does the same for DEBUG and RETURN traps
Each pipeline element runs in its own subshell (unless `lastpipe` + job control off), so `while read` in a pipeline can't set parent variables OR parent traps
Background jobs (`cmd &`) reset SIGINT and SIGQUIT to ignore in non-job-control shells — a background child may survive your Ctrl-C
A subshell's EXIT trap fires at subshell exit, giving you scoped cleanup: `( trap 'rm -f "$f"' EXIT; work )`
`exec cmd` replaces the shell image entirely — no EXIT trap runs, all handlers are gone
`$$` stays the parent's PID inside a subshell; use `$BASHPID` for the actual current subshell PID when signaling
Sourced scripts share the caller's trap table — a `trap ... EXIT` in a sourced file hijacks the caller's cleanup
Comparison row: `set -e` scope = current shell + inherited by subshells; ERR trap scope = current shell only unless `set -E`

chapters.title: Trade-offs, Costs, and Common Mistakes
points: Mistake: setting the trap before creating the resource, so a failure in between leaves the handler referencing an unset variable
Mistake: double quotes in the trap string, freezing the value at definition time instead of at fire time
Mistake: unquoted `$tmpdir` in `rm -rf` — an empty variable turns cleanup into a filesystem wipe
Mistake: trapping INT without re-raising, so the script reports success (0) after being interrupted
Mistake: assuming EXIT covers everything — SIGKILL, power loss, and `exec` all bypass it; add a startup sweep of stale temp dirs
Mistake: overwriting an earlier trap because there's only one handler slot per signal — compose into one cleanup function
Mistake: cleanup functions that themselves fail under `set -e`, silently skipping the rest of the teardown
Mistake: expensive work inside a handler — signals can arrive again mid-handler; keep handlers short and re-entrant safe
Trade-off: `trap cleanup EXIT` is simple but non-composable; a cleanup-stack array is composable but more machinery
Trade-off: killing the process group is thorough but can hit the interactive shell that launched you if you're not group leader
Trade-off: `set -euo pipefail` catches more bugs but breaks scripts that rely on non-zero returns as data — retrofit carefully
Re-entrancy: a signal arriving while the EXIT trap runs can re-enter cleanup — disarm first with `trap - EXIT INT TERM`
Race window: between `mktemp` and `trap` there are microseconds where a signal leaks the resource — it's small but real
Debug tooling: `set -x` inside the trap, or `trap 'echo DEBUG: $BASH_COMMAND' DEBUG` to trace what ran before the failure

chapters.title: Production Patterns and Summary
points: Canonical script skeleton: `set -Eeuo pipefail`, define `cleanup`, `mktemp -d`, `trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM HUP`, then do work
Disarm-first cleanup: start the handler with `trap - EXIT INT TERM` so re-entry and recursion are impossible
Preserve exit status: `cleanup(){ local rc=$?; ...; return $rc; }` — never let cleanup mask the real failure code
Signal-faithful exit: for INT, finish with `trap - INT; kill -INT "$$"` so callers see 130, not a fabricated code
Child reaping pattern: collect PIDs in an array, TERM them all, `sleep` a grace period, KILL survivors, then `wait`
Lock-file pattern: `exec 9>/var/lock/my.lock; flock -n 9 || exit 1` — the lock releases automatically when the shell dies, even on SIGKILL
Startup sweep: on launch, delete stale temp dirs older than N days matching your template, covering past SIGKILL leaks
Idempotency rule: every cleanup action must be safe to run twice and safe to run when the resource was never created
Testing traps: run the script, `kill -TERM` it from another terminal, and assert the temp dir is gone and the status is 143
`shellcheck` catches unquoted trap variables, double-quoted trap strings, and missing `set -E` — run it in CI
Summary table — EXIT: always, use for cleanup | ERR: on failure, use for diagnostics | INT: Ctrl-C, clean and re-raise | TERM: shutdown, graceful stop | KILL: uncatchable, plan for the leak
Rule of thumb: acquire, then immediately trap; disarm on entry; preserve status on exit; assume SIGKILL will eventually win
